title: Jonah runs (Jonah 1)
hookLine: told to go east, Jonah takes a ship west, and sleeps through a storm

lines: TARSHISH: THE END OF THE MAP.
cards: The call comes, and it's the last thing Jonah wants. Go to Nineveh, that great city of Assyria, the empire Israel had most reason to fear, and tell them God has seen their wickedness. Nineveh is east, overland.
So Jonah walks to the port of Joppa, finds a ship for Tarshish, somewhere far out at the western end of the known world, pays the fare, and climbs aboard. Not a no.
Just the opposite direction, as far as a ticket can take him. The story runs four short chapters, and its hero is already running.

teach.h: DOWN TO JOPPA, DOWN INTO THE SHIP.
teach.b: Read chapter one slowly and a word keeps coming back. Jonah went down to Joppa. He went down into the ship.
When the storm hits, the King James Bible says: "Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep." Down, down, down. In Hebrew it's the same verb each time.
Running from God, in this story, is a long slide downward. The ship is about to break apart. The sailors, who aren't Israelites, each cry out to their own gods and throw cargo overboard.
And Jonah, the only prophet on board, sleeps in the hold until the captain wakes him and tells him to pray.
When they cast lots and the lot falls on Jonah, he finally says who he is: "I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land."

teach.h: RUNNING FROM THE GOD OF THE SEA, BY SEA.
teach.b: He's running from the God who made the sea, by sea. He tells them to throw him overboard. And here's the detail that's easy to miss: they don't want to.

teach.h: THE SAILORS ROW TO SAVE HIM.
teach.b: They row hard for land first, trying to save him. Only when that fails do they cast him in, and the sea goes calm. The sailors end up in awe of God, offering sacrifices and making vows.

teach.h: HE LAY, AND WAS FAST ASLEEP.
teach.b: In this chapter they come off kinder and more prayerful than the prophet. That's the story's sense of humor, and its point. Jonah isn't a hero yet.
He's someone a lot of us recognize.

how: Christians read the book of Jonah as one short story, often in a single sitting; in Jewish practice the whole book is read in synagogue on the afternoon of Yom Kippur, and Christians in many churches hear it in Lent.

games.q: who did what in Jonah 1 — tap the pairs.
p: where God sent him, to the east
where he sailed, far to the west

s: Jonah said no to God out loud
he never argues in chapter one. he just buys a ticket in the opposite direction.
the sailors tried to save Jonah before throwing him overboard
they rowed hard for land first. only when that failed did they cast him in.
the word "down" keeps coming back in chapter one
down to Joppa, down into the ship, and down into its sides.

games.q: you're a sailor in a storm. the ship is breaking up, and the stranger who caused it says, throw me overboard. what do you do?
o: row hard for land, trying to save him first.
games.why: the sailors row for land first. only when the sea grows worse do they cast him in, and then they end up in awe of God.

practice: Let your mind go to the thing you keep buying a ticket away from: a conversation, a call you haven't returned, a decision, an apology.

Don't scold yourself; just name the direction you're avoiding, east, and notice how much effort west is costing you. If you pray, tell God plainly where you've been running; if not, simply say it to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Jonah runs. Called east to Nineveh, he sails west for Tarshish, and goes down, down, down, until a storm stops him.

orig.note: Hebrew: dove. the prophet's name means a bird that flies, which is just what he does.

carryVoice: Your line: you can't outrun him. In this story, running only ever goes down. See you tomorrow.
